newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Islamic group proposes Afghan truce, peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Islamic group proposes Afghan truce, peace talks.

text.p: The Organisation of Islamic Conference on Monday proposed an OIC-monitored truce in Afghanistan and a conference of warring groups in Saudi Arabia.
OIC Assistant Secretary-General for Political Affairs Ibrahim Saleh Bakr told a news conference in Islamabad that his 52-nation organisation was seeking an unconditional ceasefire.
As soon as it was agreed, all Afghan factions would be invited to meet in the Red Sea Saudi town of Jeddah.
Bakr said the OIC, which had sent him as its envoy to Afghanistan, had not set a deadline for the truce.

He said the OIC wanted observers from member states or from the United Nations to monitor the ceasefire between the radical Taleban Islamic militia and the forces of the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.
But he said no international peacekeeping force was planned because it would be too costly.

Bakr said he had met Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar and powerful northern militia chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who was also speaking on behalf of his new allies Rabbani and ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood recently.
He said both seemed interested in peace, "but they have some conditions...(Which) we want to eliminate".
He said the Taleban wanted Dostum to declare his neutrality, while Masood insisted on demilitrarising the Taleban-held capital Kabul.

Bakr said all Afghan factions would be invited to the Jeddah conference to decide on a future peace formula, including a transitional arrangement and the convening of a traditional Loya Jirga (grand assembly), or elections.
He said he had met Omar on Sunday in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar and had visited Dostum the previous day in the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif.
He said he had been unable to meet Rabbani and Masood because of communication difficulties, but Dostum had assured him that he would convey the OIC peace plan to them.
Dostum told the OIC envoy that he spoke for Rabbani and Masood as head of a newly formed supreme council for the defence of Afghanistan.
Earlier on Monday, the Taleban and their opponents said they were ready to accept a Pakistani-brokered ceasefire, but the two sides set contrasting conditions.

Dr Abdullah (one name), a spokesman for Masood said in the town of Jabal os-Siraj, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul, that the ceasefire was acceptable, but only on condition that the Afghan capital be demilitarised afterwards.
"If a ceasefire is agreed today, then talks on the demilitarisation of Kabul should start immediately," he said.
A Taleban spokesman in Kandahar said the militia had agreed to a ceasefire, but insisted that it must be followed immediately by an exchange of prisoners.

The spokesman, Syed Mohammed Haqqani, said the Taleban wanted the truce monitored by a 12-man commission. The Taleban would choose six of its members, while the rest would come from opposed factions, including those of Dostum, Masood and Shi'ite Moslem leader Karim Khalili.
If the ceasefire held, and prisoners were exchanged, peace talks could follow, Haqqani said.
